title: Georgia State's TA Pounce course chatbot raises the share of students earning an A or B by 4 percentage points in randomized trials in two online courses (2021-2023)
summary: In trials with 2,483 Georgia State students in online Government and Microeconomics courses from 2021 to 2023, the TA Pounce text chatbot raised the share earning an A or B by 4 points.
account: Georgia State University tested a course chatbot, called TA Pounce, that ran on the text-messaging platform of Mainstay, in two large asynchronous online courses. In Introduction to American Government (fall 2021, spring 2022 and fall 2022) and Principles of Microeconomics (2022-23 academic year), researchers randomly assigned half of 1,568 and 915 enrolled students to receive two or three scheduled text messages a week. The messages listed due dates, prompted students to finish assignments and encouraged them. The chatbot answered questions from a course knowledge base and passed other questions to the teaching assistant. Katharine Meyer of the Brookings Institution, Lindsay Page of Brown University and coauthors report that the chatbot raised the likelihood that students earned an A or B by four percentage points, from 61 percent in the control group, with similar results in both courses. In Microeconomics, women gained most and men showed no effect. The estimated gain in the numeric final grade, 1.58 points on a control mean of 71.07, was not statistically significant. The authors describe the chatbot as non-generative AI. Several coauthors work at Georgia State. The study appeared as an NBER working paper in July 2026 and in Economics of Education Review.
purpose: The chatbot was built to send course reminders and answer students' questions in large online courses. Better course performance was that purpose.
